0.title: Every Life a Gift from God
0.essay:
Modern medicine has brought great blessings: cures, safer childbirth, longer lives, relief from pain. It has also raised questions no earlier generation ever had to face.

New questions

When does a human life begin? May we create children in laboratories? What should be done with frozen embryos? Should parents test for disabilities before birth? May doctors help a suffering person to die?

Old principles

The Bible does not mention IVF or genetic testing. But it gives clear principles that apply to them all. Every human being is made in God’s image. Human life belongs to God, who gives it and takes it away. We are forbidden to take innocent life. And we are called to love and protect the weak: the unborn, the disabled and the dying.

Not abstract

These questions are not theoretical. Many readers have faced them personally: a difficult pregnancy, infertility, a child with a disability, a dying parent. This study tries to speak clearly and compassionately, remembering that the gospel brings forgiveness to those who have made wrong choices, and comfort to those facing hard ones.

The chapters

The Sanctity of Human Life; Life Before Birth; Infertility, IVF and Embryos; Disability and the Value of Every Life; and The End of Life.

For reflection

Which of these questions has touched your own life or family? Bring it honestly to God as you read.

1.title: The Sanctity of Human Life
1.essay:
Human worth does not depend on ability, intelligence, health, age, usefulness or being wanted. It depends on God, who made us in his image and loves us.

Made in God’s image

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Every human being, from the smallest embryo to the oldest adult, bears God’s image.

Some modern thinkers argue that only those with certain abilities, such as self-awareness or rationality, are “persons” with full rights. Scripture rejects this. Human beings are persons because God made them in his image, not because of what they can do. A simple test: do you value people according to what they can do, or according to who made them?

Life belongs to God

“See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). We do not own our lives, or anyone else’s. Job, having lost his children, worshipped and said, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). The giving and taking of life belong to God. That truth humbles us, and it comforts us: our lives are in his hands.

You shall not murder

The sixth commandment is short: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). After the flood, God explained why human life is so precious: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). Murder is an attack on God’s image. The value of human life rests on that image, not on human opinion or law.

Scripture does permit the taking of life in limited cases, such as just punishment by the state (Romans 13:4) and self-defence (Exodus 22:2). What it forbids is the deliberate killing of the innocent.

Protecting the weak

Scripture repeatedly calls God’s people to defend those who cannot defend themselves: “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8). The unborn, the disabled and the dying are among the most vulnerable people of all.

Proverbs goes further: “Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter” (Proverbs 24:11). And we cannot plead ignorance, for “does not he who weighs the heart perceive it?” (Proverbs 24:12). Indifference to innocent suffering is not neutral before God.

The midwives

In Egypt, Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys. “But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live” (Exodus 1:17). They risked their lives to protect the newborn, and God dealt well with them and gave them families. Protecting innocent life is worth great risk.

Think of a doctor pressured by colleagues to take part in a procedure that ends a human life. Remembering Exodus 1, she respectfully refuses on grounds of conscience, while continuing to care for her patients with excellence. Her integrity costs her a promotion. But she has a clear conscience before God.

Christ and the value of life

The Son of God took human flesh, beginning his human life as an embryo in Mary’s womb. He healed the sick, welcomed children, touched lepers and gave his life for sinners. The incarnation affirms the value of human life at every stage, and the cross shows how much God values even the lives of the guilty.

Common ground

Many who are not Christians also value human life, because the work of God’s law is “written on their hearts” (Romans 2:15). Christians can work alongside others to protect life, while pointing to the God who gives it its worth.

For reflection

Who are the most vulnerable people in your society? What does Proverbs 24:11–12 ask of you?

2.title: Life Before Birth
2.essay:
Scripture speaks of unborn children as persons, known and formed by God. The Son of God himself was once an embryo.

Known in the womb

David praises God: “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13). And further: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them” (Psalm 139:16). The unborn child is known and loved by God.

God told Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you” (Jeremiah 1:5). God’s relationship with a person can begin before birth. David could even speak of himself from the moment of conception: “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5).

John and Jesus

When Mary, newly pregnant with Jesus, visited Elizabeth, who was six months pregnant with John, “the baby leaped in her womb” (Luke 1:41). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, cried, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:42–43).

Both unborn children are treated as persons, and one of them is the Lord. The angel had promised that John would be “filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1:15). God’s work in a person’s life can begin before birth.

Abortion

Since unborn children are human persons made in God’s image, deliberately ending their lives is the taking of innocent human life. It is forbidden by the sixth commandment.

A disputed law

One passage is sometimes used to argue otherwise. Exodus 21 addresses a case where “men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm” (Exodus 21:22). Then the offender is fined. “But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life” (Exodus 21:23).

Some read this as a miscarriage, with a fine for the loss, and conclude that the unborn child has lower value. Others read it as a premature birth: a fine if the child survives unharmed, and life for life if there is serious harm. The premature-birth reading is more natural, since the text speaks of children coming out, not of a child dying, and then applies the principle of life for life. And even on the other reading, the passage concerns accidental harm, not deliberate killing. Scripture gives no support to abortion.

Hard cases

Some pregnancies come from rape. Some involve serious disability. Some threaten the mother’s life. These are agonising situations, and they call for great tenderness.

In cases of rape, the child is still an innocent human life. The mother needs enormous support and care, and the crime must be reported. Where a pregnancy directly threatens the mother’s life, such as an ectopic pregnancy where the child cannot survive, treating the mother to save her life is not the same as deliberately killing the child, and is permitted.

Grace for the guilty

Many women and men have been involved in abortion, often under pressure, in fear, or without understanding. Scripture offers full forgiveness through Christ: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). No one is beyond the reach of the cross. Churches must offer both truth and grace.

More than opposition

Christians should support pregnancy centres, adoption and foster care, and care for single mothers. Opposing abortion while neglecting mothers and children is inconsistent with the gospel.

Think of a teenage girl from church who becomes pregnant and is terrified. Her parents are angry at first, but her church surrounds her with love. An older couple helps with practical needs; others offer childcare later on. She keeps her baby. Years later, she says the church’s support saved two lives.

For reflection

How do Psalm 139 and Jeremiah 1 shape your view of the unborn? What practical support could you or your church give to women facing unplanned or difficult pregnancies?

3.title: Infertility, IVF and Embryos
3.essay:
Infertility is a real grief, often hidden and often lonely. Scripture is full of women who longed for children, and it treats their pain with great tenderness.

The pain of waiting

Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah and Elizabeth all longed for children. Rachel cried to Jacob, “Give me children, or I shall die!” (Genesis 30:1). Hannah wept and would not eat. “She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly” (1 Samuel 1:10).

When Eli the priest saw her lips moving without sound, he thought she was drunk. She explained, “I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:15). He blessed her, and she went away “and her face was no longer sad” (1 Samuel 1:18). Honest prayer brought peace even before the answer came. God later gave her Samuel, and her grief became praise. Churches should treat infertility with that same compassion and honesty.

Children are a gift

“Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward” (Psalm 127:3). Children are given by God, not owed to us. They are gifts, not rights or products. And every child, however conceived, is a gift to be welcomed and loved.

When Rachel demanded children, Jacob answered, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?” (Genesis 30:2). Her later attempt to gain children through her servant brought only further conflict.

Couples who long for children may pray, seek medical help and trust God’s wisdom. God “gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children” (Psalm 113:9). Many find great joy through adoption, which reflects God’s own adoption of us: “he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 1:5).

Medical help

Seeking medical treatment for infertility is not wrong. Doctors can treat many of its causes. The ethical questions arise with some assisted reproductive technologies, especially IVF.

IVF and embryos

In IVF, eggs are fertilised outside the body, creating embryos, which are then placed in the womb. Often more embryos are created than are used. Some are frozen indefinitely, some destroyed, some used for research. Since embryos are human lives made in God’s image, creating them only to discard or freeze them raises serious moral problems.

Third parties

Some techniques bring a third person into the marriage: donor eggs, donor sperm or a surrogate mother. This separates parenthood from the one-flesh union of marriage, and raises real concerns for children who may never know a biological parent.

IVF: the views

Some Christians reject IVF entirely, arguing that it separates procreation from sexual union. Others accept it freely, treating embryos as potential life rather than as persons. Many take a middle position: IVF within marriage, using the couple’s own eggs and sperm, is permissible if every embryo created is treated as a child, with none deliberately destroyed.

The middle position is wise. IVF is not forbidden in itself, but every embryo is a human life. Couples should create only as many embryos as they intend to implant, refuse the destruction of embryos, and avoid donor gametes and surrogacy, which bring a third party into the marriage. Frozen embryos already in existence can be given a chance at life through embryo adoption. And Christians who have used IVF in other ways should find grace, not condemnation.

Think of a couple who have struggled with infertility for years and decide to pursue IVF. They talk with their pastor and their doctor, and decide to create only a small number of embryos, intending to implant all of them. After their first child is born, they still have two frozen embryos, which they later implant too. Every child is welcomed as a gift.

Trusting God

Not every couple will have children, whatever they do. God’s love does not depend on fertility. To those who could have no children, God promised “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5). A childless life can be deeply fruitful in God’s kingdom.

For reflection

Is there someone in your church struggling with infertility who needs care and prayer? How does God’s adoption of us give meaning to human adoption?

4.title: Disability and the Value of Every Life
4.essay:
No life is a mistake. Scripture treats people with disabilities not as burdens, but as image-bearers, honoured guests, and indispensable members of Christ’s body.

God’s sovereignty

When Moses protested that he was not eloquent, God answered, “Who has made man’s mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11). Then he promised, “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:12).

Disability is not outside God’s purposes. That does not make disability good in itself; it is part of a fallen world. But it means no life is an accident, and God’s purposes are not limited by human weakness.

Not a punishment

The disciples asked Jesus whether a man born blind was being punished for his own sin or his parents’. Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him” (John 9:3). Then he healed him. Disability is not evidence of special guilt, and God works through it.

At the king’s table

After Jonathan’s death, King David sought someone from Saul’s family to whom he could show kindness. He found Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, who “was lame in both his feet” (2 Samuel 9:13). David said, “I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan” (2 Samuel 9:7), restored his land, and gave him a permanent place: “So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table, like one of the king’s sons” (2 Samuel 9:11).

It is a picture of the gospel: the weak, welcomed to the King’s table by grace. Jesus told a parable of a great banquet. When the invited guests refused, the master said, “bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (Luke 14:21). God’s kingdom welcomes those the world overlooks.

Indispensable

Paul says that in the church, “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). “On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22). God has put the body together so that all its members care for one another. People with disabilities are not burdens to the church but gifts to it.

God often displays his power in weakness. “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). People with disabilities often teach the whole church dependence, patience and grace.

Prenatal testing

Prenatal testing can help parents and doctors prepare to care for a child. But in many places it leads to the abortion of children diagnosed with disabilities. Christians should value every child, whatever the diagnosis, and support families caring for children with disabilities.

Think of a couple told during pregnancy that their baby has a serious genetic condition, and offered an abortion. They decline. Their church supports them through the birth and beyond. Their daughter’s life is shorter than most, but full of love. They say she taught their whole church what it means to be valued simply for who you are.

Caring for carers

Parents and families caring for people with severe disabilities often carry heavy, lifelong burdens. The church should offer practical help, respite and friendship, not just sympathy.

Belonging in the church

Churches should make it possible for people with disabilities to worship, belong and serve. That means thinking about physical access, communication, sensory needs and pastoral care. A church that is hard to enter, hard to follow or hard to belong to is quietly saying something it does not mean.

The resurrection hope

In the new creation, every disability will be healed. “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy” (Isaiah 35:5–6). That hope belongs to every believer, and it gives dignity to every life now.

For reflection

How welcoming is your church to people with disabilities and their families? What does Mephibosheth’s story teach you about God’s grace to you?

5.title: The End of Life
5.essay:
“For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die” (Ecclesiastes 3:1–2). Christians face death with hope, not denial.

A time to die

Death will come to all, and modern medicine cannot hold it off for ever. We do not control the times. Accepting that there is a time to die is not giving up on life; it is trusting God with its boundaries. “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). Christians need not fight death at any cost.

Euthanasia and assisted suicide

Some argue that suffering people should be allowed or helped to end their lives. Scripture forbids the deliberate ending of innocent life, including one’s own (Exodus 20:13). Our bodies are not finally ours: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

Euthanasia and assisted suicide, even when motivated by compassion, take into human hands what belongs to God. They also put pressure on the elderly, the sick and the disabled to feel they are a burden, and to wonder whether they have a duty to die.

Saul’s death

King Saul, badly wounded in battle, asked his armour-bearer to kill him. The armour-bearer refused, and Saul fell on his own sword (1 Samuel 31:4). Later, an Amalekite came to David claiming he had killed Saul at Saul’s own request. David did not treat it as mercy. He said, “How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” (2 Samuel 1:14). Taking a life, even at the dying person’s request, was treated as killing.

Allowing death and causing death

Christians are not required to accept every possible treatment. It is right to decline or withdraw treatments that are burdensome and offer little hope, allowing a disease to take its course. It is right to give good pain relief, even if it may shorten life as a side effect. The line is between allowing death and deliberately causing it.

Palliative care

Excellent care of the dying — relieving pain and providing comfort, companionship and spiritual support — is a Christian calling. The modern hospice movement grew largely out of Christian conviction. Dying people need presence, not abandonment.

Think of a Christian family facing their father’s final illness. Doctors propose aggressive treatment with little chance of success. After prayer and discussion, the family chooses palliative care. Their father’s pain is well managed. He spends his final weeks at home, is reconciled with his estranged son, and reads the Psalms with his grandchildren. He dies peacefully.

Suffering and meaning

Suffering at the end of life is real and hard. But it is not meaningless. “So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:16–17).

“For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). God can use even the final days of a life for good: reconciliation, witness and preparation for glory.

Job’s worship

When Job lost everything, he tore his robe, fell on the ground and worshipped. “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). “In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong” (Job 1:22). Life and death are in God’s hands, and he can be trusted with both.

Planning ahead

Christians should consider making their wishes known about end-of-life care, through conversations with family and written directions, in line with biblical principles. It is a kindness to those who will one day have to make decisions on our behalf. The Death, Dying and Heaven study covers preparing for death, grief and the Christian hope more fully.

For reflection

What is the difference between allowing death and causing death? Have you discussed your wishes for end-of-life care with your family? How does 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 give you hope?
